sources.claim: Sandakan was nicknamed 'Little Hong Kong of North Borneo' after British-encouraged Cantonese/Hakka migration built a dense shophouse port town.
Sandakan grew from the 1879 settlement; the pre-war town was totally destroyed by Allied bombing in 1944-45.
William B. Pryer moved the administration on 21 June 1879 and named the new settlement 'Elopura', meaning beautiful city.
The earlier Cowie settlement was renamed Kampong German for its German bases and burnt down accidentally on 15 June 1879.
Sandakan's Little Hong Kong identity and trading-port backstory remain a live tourism narrative in 2026.
Pre-WWII Berhala Island was a quarantine station for labourers from China and the Philippines and home to a leper colony; Japan used it as an internment camp.
On 4 June 1943 the 'Berhala Eight' POWs escaped by taking a boat from the leper colony and paddling/sailing ~250km to Tawi-Tawi, missing the Sandakan Death Marches.
Pulau Berhala, ~8km from Sandakan jetty, is being developed as a sustainable recreational-forest tourism site.
Australian and British POWs were held at the Sandakan camp during the Japanese occupation of Borneo.
Sandakan Memorial Park marks where ~2,400 Australian and British POWs died; entry is free.
Rusting WWII relics - an excavator, generator and boiler - still lie in their original positions at the former camp site.
Between Jan-Jun 1945 over 1,000 POWs were force-marched 260km from Sandakan to Ranau; about half died en route.
Masjid Jamek's timber pillars carry WWII bullet holes; land reclamation pushed the shoreline ~350m away and the heritage structure is now threatened.
Sandakan Jamek Mosque, the town's oldest mosque (opened 1890), was founded by Damsah, a Muslim cloth merchant from British India.
St Michael's is Sabah's oldest stone church; white stone was imported from Hong Kong and the Japanese dynamited it before surrender in 1945, leaving the shell standing.
St Michael's foundation stone was laid in 1893 and the church took over 30 years to complete.
Agnes Keith House (the villa 'Newlands') was home to writer Agnes Keith and her husband Harry, Conservator of Forests, who popularised 'Land Below the Wind'.
Agnes Keith House is run as a heritage museum by the Sabah Museum department.
The reconstructed bungalow displays period furniture, family photos and personal artefacts of the Keiths.
The English Tea House (opened 8 Dec 2002) sits in 1.5 acres of manicured lawn complete with a croquet pitch, beside Agnes Keith House overlooking Sandakan Bay.
The English Tea House serves fine teas, scones and cream and English/Asian fare in a colonial setting.
The self-guided Sandakan Heritage Trail starts at the ~100-year-old Masjid Jamik and climbs the 'Stairs with a Hundred Steps' to a hilltop viewpoint.
Sam Sing Kung Temple (1887) venerates the 'Three Saints', holds 100 Taoist divination poems, and its bronze bell was donated by Sandakan's first Kapitan Cina, Fung Ming Shan.
The 138-year-old temple was a religious centre for the Chinese labourers and merchants who earned Sandakan its 'Little Hong Kong' name.
Hilltop Puu Jih Shih Temple (built 1987) at Tanah Merah has a seven-tiered pagoda and commanding views over Sandakan Bay.
Puu Jih Shih is one of Sandakan's best sunset-viewing spots, with the largest Chinese temple in town.
Gomantong's caves (Simud Hitam and Simud Putih) are famous for edible swiftlet nests used in bird's-nest soup.
Licensed collectors harvest nests twice a year using only rattan ladders, ropes and bamboo poles, under strict Sabah Wildlife Department quotas.
A swirling exodus of more than 2 million bats leaves Gomantong's cave mouth each evening, roughly 5:30-6:30pm.
The Rainforest Discovery Centre is a forest education park in the Kabili-Sepilok reserve near Sandakan.
RDC has Sabah's longest canopy walkway (620m) and runs guided night walks (~RM30) to spot tarsiers, slow loris, civets and flying squirrels.
The Bornean Sun Bear Conservation Centre rehabilitates the world's smallest bears; it houses ~41 rescued ex-captive sun bears.
Sun bears, found only in Southeast Asia, are the smallest bears on Earth and are classified Vulnerable.
Labuk Bay's owner spared a 400-acre mangrove pocket from oil-palm clearance after discovering proboscis monkeys living there.
Labuk Bay Proboscis Monkey Sanctuary sits inside an oil-palm estate ~38km from Sandakan with scheduled feeding platforms.
Turtle Islands Park (40km north of Sandakan) lets overnight visitors watch a green turtle lay eggs at Selingan's hatchery; best March-October.
Evening mangrove cruises near Sandakan glide past riverbanks lit by thousands of fireflies, often with a seafood dinner.
Sandakan Crocodile Farm, 12km from town, is Malaysia's largest with ~3,000 crocodiles and a mini-zoo including a 100kg Amazonian fish.
Sandakan's UFO tart - a biscuit base topped with custard and torched meringue - is locally called Cow Dung Tart.
The UFO tart was an accidental creation (scorched meringue) by Hainanese baker Fu Ah On in 1955; 5 May is 'UFO Tart Day'.
The three-storey Sandakan Central Market's signature local dish is dry kway teow with deep-fried pork.
Sandakan's fish market is the biggest and busiest in Sabah, one of the state's most important seafood landing ports.
Buli Sim Sim is the original 1879 stilt settlement Sandakan grew from, reachable on foot by plank walkways ~3km east of town.
Buli Sim Sim has waterfront seafood restaurants, one a former fish market expanded into a floating restaurant.
Sandakan is wet year-round (~3,057mm/yr); rains ease April-June, while the NE monsoon brings >300mm/month Oct-Feb, peaking Nov-Dec.
March-May and July-August give Sandakan its driest, clearest weather for outdoor activities.
